lessons.title: Data Engineering for AI Systems
objectives: Distinguish data engineering from data analysis, database administration, backend development, CI/CD, and MLOps
Explain how data engineering changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data engineering with adjacent disciplines and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data engineering is the discipline of reliably moving and reshaping data from where it's produced to where it's consumed -- distinct from data analysis (which asks questions of data that's already arrived), database administration (which manages a single storage system's health), backend development (which serves request/response traffic, not data flow).
examples:
# five adjacent disciplines, and what makes each DIFFERENT from data engineering:
# data analysis: asks questions of data already in hand -- data engineering gets it there reliably
# DBA: keeps ONE database healthy -- data engineering moves data BETWEEN systems
# backend: serves request/response traffic -- data engineering moves data in bulk/streams
# CI/CD: deploys CODE -- data engineering moves and validates DATA
# MLOps: manages the MODEL lifecycle -- data engineering is what feeds it reliably
concepts: why AI needs reliable data infrastructure
commonMistakes: Assuming a strong model makes a strong AI system regardless of the data pipeline behind it -- most real production AI failures trace back to a data problem, not a model problem.
lessons.careerRelevance: AI Engineers are frequently the ones who have to reason about or build this pipeline, not just consume its output -- a genuinely high-leverage, distinct skill from modeling itself.

lessons.title: The Pipeline Mental Model
objectives: Describe a data pipeline's stages and the contracts that must hold between them
Explain how pipeline stages changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline stages with contracts between stages and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A data pipeline moves data through stages: a source (where data originates), ingestion (bringing it into the pipeline), transformation (reshaping it), storage (where it lands), and consumers (who use it, including AI/ML systems downstream).
examples:
# the stages, and the CONTRACT at each boundary:
# source -> ingestion: 'this is the format/schema I'll send you'
# ingestion -> transformation: 'this is what raw data looks like once it's in'
# transformation -> storage: 'this is the shape of the processed result'
# storage -> consumer: 'this is what you can rely on being there, and how fresh'
# a SILENT contract break at any boundary can produce wrong data with no crash at all
commonMistakes: Assuming a pipeline that keeps running without crashing is working correctly -- a broken contract at any stage boundary can silently produce wrong data while the pipeline appears completely.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mental model -- stages and contracts -- is the shared vocabulary data engineers use to reason about where a production data problem actually originated.

lessons.title: Batch Processing and Distributed Work
objectives: Distinguish full versus incremental batch processing and describe conceptually how distributed processing splits work
Explain how batch processing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect batch processing with full vs. incremental and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Batch processing runs on a schedule against a bounded set of data -- a full batch reprocesses everything from scratch (simple, but wasteful at scale); an incremental batch processes only what's new or changed since the last run (efficient, but requires reliably tracking what's already been processed).
examples:
# full vs. incremental batch, the trade-off:
# full: reprocess EVERYTHING every run -- simple logic, but wastes time/cost reprocessing
# unchanged data every single time
# incremental: process only what's NEW since the last successful run -- efficient,
# but requires reliably tracking a watermark/checkpoint of what's already been done
commonMistakes: Defaulting to full reprocessing 'to keep things simple' at real data volume -- this can turn a pipeline that should take minutes into one that takes hours, purely from redundant work.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this trade-off (not needing to write raw Spark code) is what lets an AI engineer reason intelligently about a data platform team's actual design choices.

lessons.title: Streaming and Event-Driven Data
objectives: Explain event streams conceptually, including event time vs. processing time and delivery semantics
Explain how event streams changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect event streams with event time vs. processing time and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Streaming processes data continuously as events arrive, rather than waiting for a batch boundary -- conceptually, producers publish events to topics (Kafka-style), and consumers read from them independently.
examples:
# event time vs. processing time -- why the distinction matters:
# a mobile event happens at 2:00pm (event time) but the device was offline and
# only sends it at 2:45pm (processing time) -- a system using processing time alone
# would misattribute WHEN this event actually occurred
#
# delivery semantics are a SPECTRUM, not just 'streaming works':
# at-most-once (may silently lose), at-least-once (may duplicate), exactly-once
# (a genuinely hard-won engineering property, not a free default)
commonMistakes: Assuming 'exactly-once' is simply how streaming systems work by default -- it's a specific, carefully-engineered property that requires deliberate design (often combined with idempotent.
lessons.careerRelevance: This event-time/processing-time distinction is a frequent, genuine source of subtle bugs in real streaming systems, and a common interview topic for data-intensive roles.

lessons.title: ETL, ELT and Choosing the Processing Location
objectives: Explain ETL vs. ELT honestly, without claiming either is universally superior
Explain how ETL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ETL with ELT and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before it's stored -- the warehouse only ever holds clean, modeled data, but transformation logic must be built and maintained outside the warehouse.
examples:
# the trade-off, stated honestly:
# ETL: warehouse only ever holds CLEAN data -- but transformation logic lives
# outside it, and reprocessing means re-running the whole external pipeline
# ELT: raw data is preserved and warehouse compute handles transformation --
# flexible, but raw/unvalidated data does sit in the warehouse before validation runs
commonMistakes: Claiming ELT is simply the modern, correct replacement for ETL -- the right choice depends on governance requirements, cost structure, and how much flexibility for reprocessing genuinely.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to justify ETL vs. ELT for a SPECIFIC scenario (not recite a general preference) is exactly the kind of grounded judgment real data engineering interviews test for.

lessons.title: Data Formats and Serialization
objectives: Explain why format choice (CSV, JSON, Parquet) affects storage and query performance
Explain how CSV changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CSV with JSON and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: CSV is simple and universally readable but has no real schema enforcement and no compression awareness. JSON supports nested, semi-structured data well but is verbose and row-oriented (every record repeats its own field names).
examples:
# why columnar (Parquet) beats row-oriented (CSV/JSON) for analytics specifically:
# query: 'average of ONE column, across 10 million rows'
# row-oriented: must read EVERY field of every row to get at that one column
# columnar (Parquet): reads ONLY that one column's data across all rows --
# often a large, direct reduction in actual bytes read for the same query
commonMistakes: Treating format choice as a minor implementation detail -- for large-scale analytical workloads, format directly determines how much data must be read for a given query, which is a real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Parquet specifically is the de facto standard format for analytical data pipelines feeding AI/ML systems at real scale.

lessons.title: Warehouses, Lakes and Lakehouses
objectives: Distinguish the storage layer, table/catalog layer, query engine, and governance layer across warehouses, lakes, and lakehouses
Explain how data warehouse changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data warehouse with data lake and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A data warehouse stores structured, modeled data optimized for fast analytical queries -- strong governance and performance, but less flexible for raw or unstructured data. A data lake stores raw data of any shape (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) cheaply at scale -- flexible, but without careful management can become disorganized ('a data swamp').
examples:
# four SEPARATE layers, often conflated into one:
# storage layer: WHERE bytes live (often cloud object storage)
# table/catalog layer: HOW raw files are organized into queryable tables
# query engine: WHAT actually executes a query against that table structure
# governance/metadata: WHO can access what, and what's tracked about it
# a lakehouse's real innovation is layering warehouse-style structure ON TOP of lake-style storage
concepts: storage vs. table vs. query-engine vs. governance layers
lessons.careerRelevance: This four-layer breakdown is exactly how real data platform architecture decisions get reasoned about and communicated across teams.

lessons.title: Partitioning and Query Efficiency
objectives: Explain partition pruning, and why partitioning is not the same concept as database indexing
Explain how partition pruning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect partition pruning with partitioning vs. indexing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Partitioning splits stored data into separate physical chunks based on a chosen key (e.g. date, region) -- when a query filters on that same key, the system can skip (prune) irrelevant partitions entirely, dramatically reducing how much data must be scanned.
examples:
# partitioning vs. indexing -- genuinely different mechanisms:
# indexing: a separate structure that speeds up lookups WITHIN one table's existing storage
# partitioning: physically SEPARATES data into chunks so a query can SKIP entire
# chunks (pruning) without reading them at all
#
# why 'more granular partitioning' isn't automatically better:
# partitioning by customer_id (millions of distinct values) creates millions of
# tiny partitions -- the small-file problem -- which can hurt performance, not help it
commonMistakes: Assuming a higher-cardinality partitioning key is always better for query performance -- an extremely high-cardinality key can create the small-file problem, actually degrading performance.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing a partitioning key that matches real, common query patterns (not just 'the most granular option') is a concrete, high-value data engineering decision.

lessons.title: Schema Evolution, Compatibility and Data Contracts
objectives: Distinguish backward-compatible from breaking schema changes, and explain the role of a data contract
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Schema Registry.
Explain how backward compatibility changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect backward compatibility with breaking changes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Schemas change over time -- new fields get added, old ones get deprecated. A backward-compatible (additive) change, like adding a new optional field, doesn't break existing consumers reading the old schema.
examples:
# additive (safe) vs. breaking (dangerous) schema changes:
# additive: adding a NEW optional field -- existing consumers reading the old
# schema are completely unaffected, since they simply ignore the new field
# breaking: renaming 'user_id' to 'customer_id', or changing its type from int
# to string -- every consumer that assumed the old name/type now silently breaks
commonMistakes: Renaming or retyping a field without warning downstream consumers -- this is one of the most common, entirely avoidable causes of a pipeline silently breaking, exactly the scenario a data.
lessons.careerRelevance: Data contracts are an increasingly standard practice at companies with multiple teams producing and consuming the same data, specifically to prevent this class of break. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Data Quality, Validation and Sensitive Data
objectives: Name the core categories of data-quality checks, and the baseline sensitive-data practices a pipeline should follow
Explain how data quality checks changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data quality checks with quality gates and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data quality checks include: null checks (are required fields present), type checks (does a field match its expected type), range checks (are values within a plausible bound), uniqueness (no unexpected duplicate keys), referential integrity (do foreign references actually resolve).
examples:
# a genuinely common, easily-missed leak point:
# a pipeline logs '{"user_id": 4471, "email": "real.email@example.com", "error": ...}'
# for debugging -- the email is now sitting in plaintext application logs,
# a real, common way sensitive data leaks that has nothing to do with the
# ACTUAL storage system's access controls at all
commonMistakes: Assuming access controls on the main data store are sufficient sensitive-data protection -- pipeline logs, error messages, and debug output are a genuinely common, separate leak point that.
lessons.careerRelevance: A quality gate that blocks bad data BEFORE it reaches an AI system is far cheaper than debugging a model that was silently trained or served on corrupted data.
lessons.explain: Data quality checks include: null checks (are required fields present), type checks (does a field match its expected type), range checks (are values within a plausible bound), uniqueness (no unexpected duplicate keys), referential integrity (do foreign references actually resolve).

lessons.title: Idempotency, Retries and Failure Recovery
objectives: Explain idempotent pipeline writes, and why a data-pipeline retry is a different concept from a CI/CD deployment retry
Explain how idempotent writes changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect idempotent writes with deduplication keys and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An idempotent pipeline write produces the same end result whether it runs once or is retried multiple times after a partial failure -- typically achieved via deduplication keys (recognizing 'I've already processed this exact record') and checkpoints (tracking exactly how far a run got before failing).
examples:
# the SAME word, 'retry,' means something structurally different here:
# CI/CD retry: re-run a DEPLOYMENT -- the code either deploys or it doesn't, cleanly
# data-pipeline retry: re-run PROCESSING of data -- without a dedup key/checkpoint,
# a naive retry can process the SAME records again, silently duplicating results
# rather than safely resuming from where the failure actually happened
commonMistakes: Assuming a pipeline retry is automatically safe the same way a CI/CD deployment retry is -- without dedup keys or checkpoints, a data-pipeline retry can silently duplicate already-processed.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is a genuinely common, real production incident category -- a retried pipeline run silently double-processing data because idempotency wasn't designed in from the start.
lessons.explain: An idempotent pipeline write produces the same end result whether it runs once or is retried multiple times after a partial failure -- typically achieved via deduplication keys (recognizing 'I've already processed this exact record') and checkpoints (tracking exactly how far a run got before failing).

lessons.title: Backfills, Reprocessing and Data Versioning
objectives: Explain what a safe backfill requires, beyond simply re-running the pipeline over old dates
Explain how backfill changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect backfill with reprocessing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A backfill reprocesses historical data -- often needed after discovering a bug in transformation logic that affected past runs.
examples:
# what makes a backfill genuinely SAFE, not just 'rerun the old dates':
# bounded: a specific date range, not open-ended reprocessing
# versioned: clear which transformation LOGIC produced which historical result
# throttled: doesn't compete for the same resources live production traffic needs
# communicated: downstream consumers who used the old wrong values should know
# a correction happened, not just silently see different numbers appear later
commonMistakes: Re-running an old pipeline over historical dates without bounding, versioning, or communicating the change -- this can silently overwrite historical results with no record of what changed or.
lessons.careerRelevance: A well-executed backfill (with a clear record of what changed and why) is a genuine trust-building action with downstream teams after a real production data bug.
lessons.explain: A backfill reprocesses historical data -- often needed after discovering a bug in transformation logic that affected past runs.

lessons.title: Pipeline Orchestration and DAGs
objectives: Explain DAG-based orchestration concepts: dependencies, schedules, retries, and failure propagation
Explain how DAG changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DAG with task dependencies and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipeline orchestration manages a set of interdependent tasks as a DAG (directed acyclic graph) -- each task has dependencies (what must succeed before it runs), a schedule (when it should run), a retry policy (what happens on failure), and conditional logic (sensors/triggers waiting for an external condition).
examples:
# failure propagation depends on the ACTUAL dependency structure, not a blanket rule:
# ingest -> validate -> transform -> feature_build -> publish (a linear chain --
# a failure anywhere stops everything downstream of it)
# a SEPARATE, independent audit_log task with no dependency on this chain
# continues running normally even if the main chain fails partway through
commonMistakes: Assuming every task in an orchestrated pipeline either all succeeds or all fails together -- failure propagation follows the ACTUAL dependency graph; independent tasks with no dependency on.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reading and reasoning about a real DAG's dependency structure (not just running it) is a core, practical data engineering skill.

lessons.title: Feature Pipelines for Machine Learning
objectives: Explain offline vs. online features, and the specific mechanisms that cause training/serving skew
Explain how offline vs. online features changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect offline vs. online features with feature store (conceptual) and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Offline features are computed in batch, often over large historical windows, and used for training. Online features are computed in real time (or near-real time) and used for live inference.
examples:
# training/serving skew, and the SEPARATE point-in-time leakage problem:
# training/serving skew: offline feature uses avg(txn, 30 DAYS); online feature
# uses avg(txn, 30 HOURS) by a copy-paste mistake -- SAME name, DIFFERENT formula
# point-in-time leakage: a training example for 'March 1st' accidentally includes
# a transaction from March 15th -- data that wouldn't have existed yet at that
# point in time, silently inflating the model's apparent training performance
commonMistakes: Assuming a model trained on 'the same feature' will behave identically in production -- if the offline and online computation paths differ even subtly (formula, source, version), the model.
lessons.careerRelevance: Training/serving skew is one of the most common, hard-to-diagnose real production ML bugs -- directly connecting this course to MLOps's own model-monitoring concerns.

objectives: Apply general observability principles specifically to data pipelines, and synthesize the course's core mindset

Connect data lineage with freshness SLI/SLO and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Data lineage traces where a specific value came from -- which source, through which transformations, to reach this final number -- essential for tracing an incorrect downstream result back to its actual origin.

lessons.careerRelevance: This closing synthesis directly connects Data Engineering into MLOps's own production-AI mindset -- the two disciplines are genuinely part of the same overall system, not separate concerns.

lessons.title: Apache Kafka: topics, partitions & consumer groups
objectives: Explain Kafka producers, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, and delivery guarantees
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Kafka Connect.
Explain how Kafka changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Kafka with topic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Kafka is a durable distributed event log. Producers append records to topic partitions; ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not globally across a topic.
lessons.example: A payment event key can be account_id so events for one account stay ordered in one partition. Multiple consumers in one group process different partitions. If processing succeeds before committing the offset, a crash can cause the message to be delivered again, so handlers should be idempotent.
commonMistakes: Assuming Kafka gives exactly-once business behavior automatically.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

examples: A payment event key can be account_id so events for one account stay ordered in one partition. Multiple consumers in one group process different partitions. If processing succeeds before committing the offset, a crash can cause the message to be delivered again, so handlers should be idempotent.

lessons.title: Apache Airflow: DAGs, scheduling, retries & backfills
objectives: Design an Airflow DAG with dependencies, retries, idempotent tasks, and safe backfills
Explain how Airflow changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Airflow with DAG and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Airflow orchestrates scheduled workflows as directed acyclic graphs. A DAG describes dependencies; the scheduler decides when runnable tasks should execute; workers run tasks.
lessons.example: Daily pipeline: extract_orders -> validate_orders -> transform_orders -> load_partition -> publish_quality_report. Configure bounded retries with delay, and make each task safe to rerun for the same logical date.
commonMistakes: Putting all business logic in one giant Airflow task.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

examples: Daily pipeline: extract_orders -> validate_orders -> transform_orders -> load_partition -> publish_quality_report. Configure bounded retries with delay, and make each task safe to rerun for the same logical date.

exercises.title: Choose ETL or ELT for warehouse loading
exercises.prompt: A team needs strict governance -- only validated, clean data may ever land in the shared warehouse. Should they choose ETL or ELT?
exercises.hint: ETL -- transformation happens before loading, so the warehouse only ever holds clean, validated data, matching the strict governance requirement

exercises.title: Choose batch or streaming for nightly training data
exercises.prompt: A recommendation model retrains once per night using the previous day's activity. What processing approach fits, and why?
exercises.hint: scheduled batch -- the use case tolerates a full day of latency, and batch is simpler and cheaper than streaming when that tolerance exists

exercises.title: Choose batch or streaming for real-time fraud features
exercises.prompt: A fraud-detection model needs a feature reflecting a transaction within milliseconds of it occurring. What processing approach fits?
exercises.hint: continuous streaming -- the sub-second latency requirement rules out batch or even micro-batch

exercises.title: Choose processing approach for an analytics dashboard
exercises.prompt: A dashboard needs to reflect activity within about 5 minutes, but doesn't need sub-second freshness. What approach fits, and why not full streaming?
exercises.hint: micro-batch -- 5-minute tolerance doesn't require continuous streaming's added operational complexity, but is too tight for a once-daily batch

exercises.title: Diagnose a breaking schema change
exercises.prompt: A source system renames a field from `user_id` to `customer_id` with no notice. Several downstream pipelines start failing. What's the root cause, and what should have prevented it?
exercises.hint: a breaking (non-additive) schema change with no coordination; a data contract between producer and consumer would have made the compatibility expectation explicit and required a coordinated rollout

exercises.title: Design a schema-evolution plan using a data contract
exercises.prompt: Design a plan to safely rename a field, keeping existing consumers working during the transition.
exercises.hint: support both the old and new field names simultaneously for a transition period (an additive step), update consumers to use the new name, then remove the old name only after confirming no consumer still depends on it

exercises.title: Design a data-quality gate
exercises.prompt: Design a quality gate for an incoming customer dataset that checks nulls, types, uniqueness, and ranges. What should happen when a check fails?
exercises.hint: the gate should block affected records (or the whole batch, depending on severity) from propagating downstream, log the specific violation, and route failing records to a review/dead-letter path rather than silently dropping or passing them through

exercises.title: Diagnose a non-idempotent pipeline
exercises.prompt: A pipeline fails partway through a run. It's retried, and downstream tables now show duplicate records. What's the likely cause, and the fix?
exercises.hint: the pipeline lacks idempotent writes -- no deduplication key or checkpoint to recognize already-processed records; fix by adding a dedup key and/or checkpointing progress so a retry doesn't reprocess already-completed work

exercises.title: Design a safe backfill
exercises.prompt: A transformation bug affected the last 30 days of processed data. Design a safe backfill plan.
exercises.hint: bound the backfill to the specific known 30-day range, use a versioned/fixed transformation so it's clear which logic produced the corrected results, throttle it to avoid competing with live production traffic, and communicate the correction to downstream consumers

exercises.title: Choose a partitioning key for a query pattern
exercises.prompt: Most queries against a large events table filter by a specific day. What partitioning key fits, and why?
exercises.hint: event_date -- matching the actual query pattern lets the system prune to just the relevant day's partition instead of scanning the whole table

exercises.title: Diagnose an over-partitioning problem
exercises.prompt: A team partitions a table by customer_id (millions of distinct values) and query performance gets WORSE, not better. What's happening?
exercises.hint: the small-file problem -- an extremely high-cardinality partitioning key creates millions of tiny partitions, and the overhead of managing/scanning that many small partitions can outweigh any pruning benefit

exercises.title: Diagnose training/serving skew
exercises.prompt: A model performs well in offline evaluation but poorly in production. Investigation shows the offline feature uses a 30-day average while the online feature (same name) uses a 30-hour average. What's this called, and what's the fix?
exercises.hint: training/serving skew -- the two paths compute a differently-defined 'same' feature; fix by centralizing the feature definition (conceptually, a feature store) so both paths compute it identically

exercises.title: Identify point-in-time leakage
exercises.prompt: A training dataset for predicting March 1st churn accidentally includes a customer interaction from March 15th. What's wrong, and what does it cause?
exercises.hint: point-in-time leakage -- the training example includes data that wouldn't have existed yet at the prediction time, artificially inflating apparent model performance during training that won't hold up in production

exercises.title: Distinguish a data-pipeline retry from a CI/CD deployment retry
exercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why retrying a failed data pipeline run is a fundamentally different concern than retrying a failed CI/CD deployment.
exercises.hint: a CI/CD retry re-runs a code deployment, which either succeeds or fails cleanly; a data-pipeline retry re-runs data processing, which -- without idempotency (dedup keys/checkpoints) -- can silently duplicate already-processed records rather than safely resuming

exercises.title: Build a DAG dependency order
exercises.prompt: Given tasks ingest, validate, transform, feature_build, publish, and an independent audit_log task, build the correct dependency order and identify which task is unaffected if transform fails.
exercises.hint: ingest -> validate -> transform -> feature_build -> publish, in that linear dependency chain; audit_log has no dependency on this chain and continues running normally even if transform fails

exercises.title: Choose CSV, JSON, or Parquet for a workload
exercises.prompt: An analytical query needs to average one column across 10 million rows, run repeatedly. Which format fits best, and why?
exercises.hint: Parquet -- its columnar layout lets the query read only that one column across all rows, rather than reading every field of every row as a row-oriented format like CSV or JSON would require

exercises.title: Trace incorrect downstream data using lineage
exercises.prompt: A dashboard shows an incorrect total. Using a lineage description (source table -> transformation A -> transformation B -> dashboard), explain how you'd trace the root cause.
exercises.hint: walk the lineage backward from the dashboard through transformation B, then A, then the source table, checking each stage's output against expectations until the point where the value first becomes wrong is identified

exercises.title: Define a freshness target for an AI consumer
exercises.prompt: A real-time fraud model consumes a feature pipeline. What freshness target would you set, and how would you justify it?
exercises.hint: a tight freshness target (e.g. seconds, not hours) justified by the fraud model's need to act on near-real-time transaction data -- a stale feature could mean the model is scoring based on outdated information during an active fraud attempt

quiz.q: How does data engineering primarily differ from data analysis?
options: They are the same discipline
Data engineering reliably moves and reshapes data to where it's needed; data analysis asks questions of data already in hand
Data analysis is a subset of MLOps
Data engineering only concerns databases

quiz.q: How does data engineering primarily differ from MLOps?
options: They are unrelated disciplines
MLOps manages the model lifecycle, generally assuming the data it needs already arrives reliably; data engineering is what makes that arrival reliable
MLOps is a subset of data engineering with no distinct concerns
Data engineering only handles model versioning

quiz.q: What is the key difference between event time and processing time?
options: They are always identical
Event time is when something actually happened; processing time is when the pipeline observed it -- these can differ, especially for late events
Processing time is always earlier than event time
This distinction only matters for batch processing

quiz.q: Is 'exactly-once' delivery a default guarantee of streaming systems?
options: Yes, always by default
No -- it's a specific, carefully-engineered property requiring deliberate design, not an automatic guarantee
Only batch systems can achieve exactly-once
Exactly-once is impossible in any distributed system

quiz.q: What is the main structural difference between ETL and ELT?
options: They are identical in practice
ETL transforms data before loading it; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it afterward, often within the warehouse
ETL only works with streaming data
ELT never uses a warehouse

quiz.q: Is ELT universally superior to ETL?
options: Yes, ELT is always the modern, correct choice
No -- the right choice depends on governance requirements, cost, and flexibility needs for the specific pipeline
ETL is always superior instead
Both are functionally identical, so it doesn't matter

quiz.q: Why is Parquet often preferred for large-scale analytical queries over CSV or JSON?
options: Parquet files are always smaller regardless of content
Its columnar layout lets a query read only the needed columns, rather than every field of every row
CSV cannot be compressed at all
JSON is always faster to parse

quiz.q: What is a genuine limitation of CSV as a data format?
options: It has no real schema enforcement and no compression awareness
It cannot represent numbers
It is always slower to write than Parquet
It cannot be read by any modern tool

quiz.q: What distinguishes a data lake from a data warehouse?
options: They are the same thing with different names
A lake stores raw data of any shape cheaply at scale; a warehouse stores structured, modeled data optimized for fast analytical queries
A warehouse can only store CSV files
A lake always has stronger governance than a warehouse

quiz.q: What is a lakehouse's key architectural idea?
options: Replacing all warehouses entirely
Layering warehouse-style table structure and query performance on top of lake-style cheap storage
Storing data exclusively in relational databases
Eliminating the need for a query engine

quiz.q: What does partition pruning allow a query to do?
options: Nothing meaningful
Skip entire irrelevant partitions instead of scanning all stored data
Automatically fix data quality issues
Delete old data automatically

quiz.q: Why can partitioning by an extremely high-cardinality key like customer_id hurt performance?
options: It never hurts performance
It can create the small-file problem -- millions of tiny partitions whose management overhead outweighs pruning benefits
High-cardinality keys are illegal as partition keys
It always improves performance instead

quiz.q: What distinguishes an additive schema change from a breaking one?
options: There is no real distinction
An additive change (like a new optional field) doesn't affect existing consumers; a breaking change (rename/retype/remove) can silently break them
Breaking changes are always intentional and communicated
Additive changes are always breaking too

quiz.q: What does a data contract provide between a producer and consumer team?
options: Nothing of practical value
An explicit, verifiable agreement about expected schema and compatibility guarantees, rather than an implicit assumption
A legal document with no technical content
A guarantee that no schema will ever change

quiz.q: What does an idempotent pipeline write guarantee?
options: The pipeline never fails
Running the write once or retrying it after a partial failure produces the same end result
The pipeline runs faster
Data quality checks are unnecessary

quiz.q: Why is a data-pipeline retry fundamentally different from a CI/CD deployment retry?
options: They are functionally identical concepts
A CI/CD retry re-runs a code deployment; a data-pipeline retry re-runs data processing, which without idempotency can silently duplicate records
CI/CD retries are always riskier
Data pipelines never need to be retried

quiz.q: When a task fails in a DAG-orchestrated pipeline, what happens to an independent task with no dependency on it?
options: It also fails automatically
It continues running normally, since failure propagation follows the actual dependency structure
The entire DAG is cancelled regardless
It retries the failed task automatically

quiz.q: What makes a backfill genuinely safe, beyond simply re-running old dates?
options: Nothing extra is needed
Being bounded to a specific date range, using a versioned transformation, throttled to avoid competing with production, and communicated to downstream consumers
Backfills are inherently always safe
Running it during peak production traffic for speed

quiz.q: What causes training/serving skew?
options: The model architecture itself
Offline and online paths computing a feature with subtly different formulas, sources, or transformation versions
Using too much training data
Insufficient GPU compute

quiz.q: What does point-in-time correctness in a training dataset prevent?
options: Slow query performance
A training example accidentally including data that wouldn't have existed yet at that historical moment, artificially inflating apparent performance
Data format incompatibility
Streaming delivery duplication

interviewPreparation.q: Explain ETL versus ELT and when you would choose each.
interviewPreparation.a: ETL transforms data before loading it, so the warehouse only ever holds clean, validated data -- suited to strict governance needs. ELT loads raw data first and transforms afterward, often pushing computation into the warehouse -- more flexible for reprocessing but requires care since raw, unvalidated data sits in the warehouse before validation runs. Neither is universally superior; the choice depends on governance, cost, and flexibility needs.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you handle schema evolution without breaking downstream consumers?
interviewPreparation.a: Distinguish additive changes (safe -- new optional fields don't affect existing consumers) from breaking changes (renaming, retyping, or removing fields). For a breaking change, support both old and new forms during a transition period, update consumers, and only remove the old form once nothing depends on it -- ideally formalized as an explicit data contract between producer and consumer teams.

interviewPreparation.q: What causes training/serving skew, and how do you prevent it?
interviewPreparation.a: It happens when the offline (training) and online (serving) computation paths compute a feature that's supposed to be identical but subtly differs -- a different formula, data source, or transformation version. Preventing it means centralizing the feature definition (conceptually, a feature store) so both paths compute the exact same logic, rather than maintaining two separate implementations that can silently drift apart.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you make a data pipeline safely re-runnable?
interviewPreparation.a: Design idempotent writes using deduplication keys (recognizing already-processed records) and checkpoints (tracking exactly how far a run got). This matters because a data-pipeline retry re-runs data processing, not a code deployment -- without idempotency, a naive retry can duplicate already-processed records rather than safely resuming from the actual failure point.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide between batch, micro-batch, and streaming?
interviewPreparation.a: It depends on the actual latency tolerance and operational complexity the use case can bear -- a nightly training job tolerates a full day of latency and fits scheduled batch; a dashboard needing few-minute freshness fits micro-batch; a real-time fraud feature needing sub-second freshness requires continuous streaming. There's no universally correct choice -- it's a genuine trade-off based on the specific requirement.

capstone.title: Design a Production Data Pipeline Feeding an AI System
capstone.description: Design a complete production-quality data pipeline -- from source systems through downstream AI/ML consumption -- for a realistic scenario, with explicit engineering trade-off decisions rather than simply following a template.
deliverables: Lake, warehouse, or lakehouse placement, justified
Offline and/or online feature consumption design
At least 3 explicit trade-off explanations, including batch vs. streaming, ETL vs. ELT, and storage format or partitioning strategy
One deliberately simplified or manual component, with justification
One realistic limitation of the overall design
capstone.portfolioTips: The required trade-off explanations are what distinguish a genuine capstone from a template exercise -- explicitly stating what you sacrificed and why is exactly the depth real data engineering and AI infrastructure interviews are testing for.
